articles.title: North Carolina State University researchers turn laser beams into a lightsaber-like antenna that sends radio signals without metal and boosts reception by 2.5 times
articles.summary: Researchers at North Carolina State University have demonstrated a laser-powered plasma antenna that transmits radio signals without a conventional metal
articles.body: Researchers at North Carolina State University have demonstrated a laser-powered plasma antenna that transmits radio signals without a conventional metal radiating element. Resembling a lightsaber, the device uses a laser to ionise air and create a thin plasma filament that transmitted a 30 MHz radio signal during laboratory tests. According to the study published in the IEEE Journal, titled ‘Laser-Induced-Plasma-Filament Antenna Transmitting 30 MHz VHF’, the received signal strength increased by approximately 2.5 times when the plasma filament was used as an antenna. The technology could eventually support reconfigurable antennas for satellites and aircraft, although further development is needed.How does the laser-powered plasma antenna workThe antenna relies on a process in which a laser beam ionises air, producing a narrow channel of plasma known as a laser-induced plasma filament. The research paper explains that electrons become concentrated around the filament’s outer edges, giving the structure characteristics similar to those of a conventional electrical conductor. When electromagnetic energy is coupled into the filament, these electrons can support the propagation and radiation of electromagnetic waves.The researchers used a laser with a pulse duration of 100 femtoseconds, a repetition rate of 1 kilohertz and a pulse energy of approximately 5 millijoules. A converging lens with a focal length of two metres was used to produce a plasma filament measuring approximately 20 centimetres in length and 0.1 millimetres in diameter. These dimensions describe the experimental prototype rather than the larger antenna structures the researchers hope to develop in the future.Plasma antenna transmits radio signals without direct contactOne of the main challenges was introducing a radio-frequency signal into the plasma filament without disrupting its structure. A conventional metal connection would distort the filament and interfere with its formation, so the researchers developed a capacitively coupled antenna feed that transfers electromagnetic energy without making direct contact with the plasma.The feed consists of a metal structure that generates an electromagnetic field around the filament. A radio-frequency generator supplies a 30 MHz signal to this structure, allowing the field to couple energy into the plasma. The resulting electromagnetic waves propagate along the filament and radiate outwards. The feed itself also has radiation characteristics, making it necessary for the researchers to distinguish its contribution from that of the plasma antenna.To test the arrangement, the team measured the received signal under two conditions. First, the laser was blocked, leaving the radio-frequency feed operating without the plasma filament. The researchers then repeated the measurements with the laser unblocked and the plasma filament present. A receiving antenna was positioned approximately five centimetres from the transmitter, with both antennas sharing the same linear polarisation and orientation.How did researchers achieve 150% stronger radio signalsThe experimental results showed that the received signal was stronger when the plasma filament was present and capacitively fed than when the laser was blocked. According to the research paper’s abstract, the received signal strength increased by approximately 2.5 times, equivalent to a reported increase of 150%, compared with the feed-only configuration.The researchers reported that the measurements supported the feasibility of using a laser-induced plasma filament as an antenna capable of radiating its own electromagnetic field. The conclusion of the paper states that the experiment represents the first demonstration of this concept to the authors’ knowledge. The work establishes a proof of concept for transmitting a 30 MHz radio-frequency signal; it does not demonstrate a fully developed antenna ready for operational use.The researchers noted that the laboratory-scale antenna had relatively low gain and lacked the beamforming precision required for operational synthetic-aperture radar systems or satellite and aircraft applications. Further work will focus on improving the antenna’s radiation performance, increasing the efficiency of the contactless feed and developing more accurate methods for characterising its electromagnetic properties.How could plasma antennas improve satellite communicationsThe researchers are investigating whether laser-induced plasma filament antennas could eventually be used in satellites and aircraft. Antenna length influences the frequencies at which radio waves can be transmitted and received, but changing the length of a conventional antenna can be difficult in applications where space, weight and mechanical deployment are important constraints.Because the plasma filament is generated by a laser, its length can be controlled through the laser’s operating parameters. The NC State news release also describes the possibility of changing the filament’s direction by steering the laser beam. This could provide a means of adjusting antenna orientation without physically moving a conventional antenna structure. However, these capabilities are potential applications of the technique rather than fully demonstrated operational functions of the current prototype.How could plasma antennas transmit and receive radio signalsThe research paper discusses the longer-term possibility of producing plasma filaments several metres long or more for high-frequency and very-high-frequency applications, as well as very-low-frequency systems. It also identifies the possibility of using the same configuration as a receiving antenna, based on electromagnetic reciprocity; this capability remains to be validated in future work. The demonstration therefore establishes an initial step towards antennas whose radiating elements can be generated and reconfigured using laser-produced plasma. The researchers' next task is to improve performance and address the technical limitations that remain before the technology can be considered for practical satellite or aircraft systems.

articles.title: GM to close Detroit battery assembly plant, but not for reasons you might think | TechCrunch
articles.summary: GM is shuttering the Brownstown Battery Assembly Plant, though the closure has nothing to do with the automaker's electrification strategy.
articles.body:
GM is closing a battery assembly plant south of Detroit, a spokesperson confirmed to TechCrunch.

The Brownstown Battery Assembly Plant assembled battery packs for Cadillac’s flagship EV, the Celestiq, and both electric drive units (the motors that power the car) and battery packs for the Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray, a plug-in hybrid version of its famous sports car. Automotive News first reported the closure.

The closure is not related to GM’s electric vehicle strategy, the spokesperson said. Instead, GM leased the site, and the lease was nearing its end.

The employees and work at Brownstown will be moved to other GM facilities, though the company would not confirm which ones.

Like many automakers, GM’s electrification strategy was thrown a curveball after the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the sweeping federal law signed last year, repealed incentives to produce and sell EVs.

Since then, the company has pared back its public comments on EVs , though it hasn’t given up on full electrification.

GM continues to produce a range of EVs, including the Chevrolet Silverado EV and the limited-time-only Chevrolet Bolt . It also continues researching new battery chemistries, including lithium-manganese-rich and sodium-ion , and it’s rolling out a new $900 million facility to speed commercialization.

articles.title: TikTok has started censoring searches for popular peptides
articles.summary: Searches for certain peptides suddenly show no results in TikTok searches, while claims of a wholesale ban are unsupported.
articles.body: Trying to pull up information for certain peptides on TikTok is now returning a “no results found” page when searching for terms like semaglutide, BPC-157, retratutide, and others. That hasn’t entirely erased visibility on TikTok for peptides, which are combinations of amino acids that include substances like insulin and GLP-1. The problem is peptides also include unregulated, unapproved substances that proponents like RFK Jr. say can assist with everything from weight loss to wound healing, despite a lack of clinical data supporting such claims. As a result, on social media platforms like TikTok, an army of influencer proponents are happy to suggest affiliated compounding pharmacies and other sources of unknown quality for drugs that people probably aren’t telling their doctors about. Bryan Johnson-connected influencer Jeff Tang alerted people about the apparent changes by TikTok in a tweet last night, before posting a video pointing blame at Eli Lilly. For now, searching for “peptides” on TikTok still pulls up plenty of short videos, and there’s no sign that actual videos have been removed, either. TikTok’s US owner didn’t respond immediately when asked for comment by The Verge. While the two ingredients of the so-called “Wolverine” peptide stack, BPC-157 and TB-500, aren’t searchable on TikTok, slight variations of either name still pull up published videos, and TikTok’s own search suggestions offered functional variations before I was even done typing any of the more popular peptides in circulation.

articles.title: Oura adds two new cardiovascular health tracking features to its smart rings
articles.summary: Oura’s new health tracking features measure how hard a user’s cardiovascular system worked during exercise, and whether their endurance is improving over time.
articles.body: Oura is introducing two new cardiovascular-focused health tracking features to its smart rings designed to help users better understand the effect regular workouts and exercise are having on their long-term health, and whether they need to ramp it up or dial things down. Cardio Effort and automatic VO2 Max (previously known as Cardio Capacity) are available for the Oura Ring Gen 3 and later models, but only to users with an active Oura membership. Instead of measuring how fast or far a user went during a run or bike ride, or metrics like calories burned, Cardio Effort measures how hard their cardiovascular system was working during exercise and how long that effort was sustained. Cardio Effort is calculated for individual workouts taking into account both intensity and duration but provides a plain language evaluation that compares a user’s cumulative weekly effort against a personalized baseline. One one end of the scale is a Light rating that’s described as being a “substantially lower cardiovascular strain than your usual baseline.” The rating scale progresses through Fair, Maintaining, Building, and Reaching at the other end which means your weekly Cardio Effort had a “markedly higher exposure relative to your baseline, signaling that it may be time to prioritize recovery.” So instead of always pushing a user to increase their efforts, the feature does make recommendations for rest when it may be more beneficial. Oura Rings already support VO2 Max readings that are used to track aerobic capacity, but the previous Cardio Capacity feature was somewhat cumbersome because estimating a user’s maximum oxygen uptake required a six-minute walking test for calibration. The new version, automatic VO2 Max, currently available as a beta feature through Oura Labs, automatically activates after users complete five “qualifying GPS-enabled activities” that include walks, runs, and hikes. Once activated VO2 Max readings will be available in the Oura app’s My Health Heart Hub section with a user’s current estimate, their capacity rated as low, fair, high, or peak, how their aerobic capacity has changed over time, and personalized insights for when VO2 Max “meaningfully shifts or stays consistent.”

articles.title: SpaceX says big AI growth fueled revenue jump
articles.summary: SpaceX announced its Q3 earnings on Tuesday, its second earnings report since going public in June.
articles.body: SpaceX announced revenues of $14.6 billion in its Q3 earnings on Tuesday, which it says was a growth of 161 percent year-over-year “fueled by our Super Intelligence (SI) segment and accelerated growth in Connectivity.” While its Space division posted a $7 million loss in income from operations, its Connectivity group posted income from operations $2.4 billion and its SI group posted $431 million. The company’s so-called “SI” business saw revenues of $7.6 billion, which were up 830 percent year-over-year, “primarily driven” by “the activation of new cloud services agreements, the acquisition of Cursor, and increased Grok adoption across enterprise customers and consumers.” For its Connectivity business, SpaceX reported revenues of $5.2 billion and 13.6 million Starlink consumer subscribers. Space business revenues were $1.8 billion, up six percent year-over-year. SpaceX is livestreaming a video of its earnings call on X. This is the second earnings report from SpaceX after the company’s IPO in June. The earnings follow a busy Q3 for Elon Musk’s rocket, AI, and social media company, which included the official closing of its $60 billion deal to acquire AI coding tool Cursor, the 13th launch of SpaceX’s Starship, and the launch of a new V5 Starlink residential dish. During the Q2 earnings call, president Gwynne Shotwell described plans to build out a terrestrial mobile network to compete with T-Mobile, AT&T and Verizon. In SpaceX’s Q2 earnings, the company also noted that its “connectivity” business, which encompasses Starlink, didn’t have a loss from operations, while its AI and space businesses did. Tesla, where Musk is also CEO, reports earnings on Wednesday.

articles.title: SpaceX’s AI business is beating expectations
articles.summary: SpaceX hit profitably in the third-quarter, with net income of $4.4 billion. AI was the engine.
articles.body:
SpaceX’s data centers and Grok agents were more profitable than investors expected in third quarter of the year, as the company leaves its roots as a space company behind to focus on artificial intelligence, which now makes up 52% of its income.

CEO Elon Musk’s deep tech conglomerate reported $14.6 billion in third-quarter revenue on Tuesday, according to its regulatory filing .

That number was driven by growth in all segments, but especially its renamed “Super Intelligence” business line, which generated $7.5 billion in revenue from the recently acquired Cursor coding tool, Grok bot, and most importantly, the company’s burgeoning neocloud business, which now boasts 1.7 GW of compute. The AI business generated $431 million in profit, which would have been higher without $1.2 billion in one-time stock-based compensation expenses related to the Cursor acquisition.

The top-line revenue number was also boosted by about $1 billion in income related to the recovery of Bitcoin prices and unspecified related-party income that might be attributed to a SpaceX investment in another company.

The growing revenue is balanced against total capital expenditures of $19.6 billion, as SpaceX continues to build out a second data center project, Colossus II, and increase investment in Starship, the heavy-lift rocket it sees as vital to deploying a new generation of Starlink satellites and developing orbital data centers. CFO Bret Johnsen said the company would spend $35 billion to $40 billion on new capital investments in the fourth quarter.

During a live-streamed discussion of the results with investors, Musk said he was spending four days a week in Memphis, Tennessee, the site of Colossus II, working to bring the data center online.

“People are starting to realize [that] the constraint on deployment of of super intelligence is more in power and cooling and infrastructure than it is in chips,” Musk argued, saying that he had tasked a team of SpaceX engineers to solve that problem. “This is a bit like the New York Yankees playing in Little League. It’s not fair, but the net result is being able to deploy power cooling infrastructure at a rate that is vastly faster than any anyone else.”

In one example, Musk noted that manufacturers of turbines to power data centers are facing 12 to 18 month delays in obtaining the metals blades and vanes required for those machines. Now, SpaceX is using the metal casting capabilities developed for SpaceX to make those components and obtain turbines more quickly.

Musk also said that the next test flight of the Starship rocket, expected in November, would see SpaceX attempt to recover both the first-stage booster and the second stage. Recovering both segments of the vehicle would be a “massive technology milestone,” Musk said, but the true milestone will be reflying both stages.

SpaceX also saw growth in subscribers to its Starlink space internet network, reaching 13.6 million consumers, with Musk predicting that the growth of AI agents would lead to more demand for connectivity.

Despite of those capital expenditures, the company’s revenue boost was substantial enough to push it back into profitability. SpaceX reported net income of $4.4 billion, a turnaround from the $1 billion loss in the same quarter last year. It will still have some catching up to do if it wants to remain profitable for the year, however. In the first nine months of the year, SpaceX still had a net income loss of $413 million.

Musk took a particularly bullish stance on the company’s Super Intelligence business segment, predicting that SpaceX’s annual recurring revenue by the end of 2027 will be “somewhere between $500 billion and $1 trillion.”

More concretely, Johnsen forecast total revenue for the first quarter of 2027 in the range of $33 billion to $37 billion.

This is a developing story. TechCrunch will update.

articles.title: SpaceX will try catching Starship and its booster for first time, Musk says
articles.summary: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said the company would try catching Starship and its booster in November for the first time.
articles.body: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said the company would attempt to catch Starship and its booster next month, with the goal of recovering the entire orbital launch system for the first time. If successful, Musk said, the attempt would mark the first time in history an orbital launch vehicle has been fully recovered. “This is a profound technology milestone in the history of civilization consciousness,” he said during the company’s third quarter earnings report Tuesday. But he also allowed for the possibility of a failure. “Success is not guaranteed on these first flights, but I’d say it’s more likely than not that this succeeds next flight,” Musk said. “And if not, we have a steady stream of Starship flight attempts through the end of this year and then accelerating next year.” "“Success is not guaranteed on these first flights, but I’d say it’s more likely than not that this succeeds next flight.”" - Elon Musk Starship is a two-stage system, composed of the Super Heavy booster (first stage) and the Starship spacecraft (second stage). It stands approximately 120 meters (around 400 feet) tall with a 9-meter diameter, and is powered by SpaceX’s Raptor engines burning liquid methane and liquid oxygen. Starship, which was first introduced in 2018, was designed to return to the launch site, where launch towers with mechanical “chopstick” arms catch the vehicle mid-air. Last month’s Starship launch represented two firsts for its next gen rocket: send the spacecraft into Earth orbit, and insert a few dozen of SpaceX’s larger and more capable V3 satellites into the Starlink constellation for the first time. Still, the launch wasn’t without its snafus: one Raptor engine shut down prematurely during ascent, prompting mission control to adapt and complete the climb on remaining. Because of the issue, SpaceX cut the planned 10-hour, 6-orbit mission short after about 3 hours and 2 Earth orbits. The Super Heavy booster splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico, while the Starship upper stage executed a de-orbit burn and ended with a fiery vertical splashdown in the Pacific Ocean north of Hawaii. articles.title: Elon Musk says Tesla-SpaceX merger being considered
articles.summary: Musk says special committees within both companies have been formed to look at a possible mega-merger.
articles.body:
Elon Musk has said he likes the idea of a merger of Tesla and SpaceX, two of his most notable companies, and it is under active consideration.

"Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said during a call with financial analysts over the quarterly business results of SpaceX on Tuesday.

While Musk noted the certainty of such a merger should not be assumed, and it would need shareholders' support, he said special committees within both companies have been formed to examine the move.

"The special committees have not reached agreement on terms of any transaction and there's no guarantee that they will," Musk added. "But I do think there is a lot of merit to merging and a lot to be gained."

With Tesla valued roughly $1.5 trillion and SpaceX valued at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history.

Shares of SpaceX rose 8% in after hours trading.

The company, which builds space rockets and Starlink internet satellites, is now expanding into offering cloud compute capacity for other tech companies, like Anthropic and Google.

That line of business has become the most profitable part of SpaceX, bringing in $7.5bn according to the latest quarterly results. Starlink also tallied revenue of $5.2bn.

SpaceX as a whole, however, is not profitable and has lost $1.1bn so far this year.

Shares of Tesla, which reports its own quarterly results on Wednesday, rose 2% after being down slightly for weeks.

Over the last year, Musk has taken to bringing more of his various companies under fewer banners. Before it went public earlier this year, SpaceX acquired xAI and X , the platform formerly known as Twitter, both of which Musk owned.

The recent launch of Terafab, a combined effort to manufacture computer chips between Tesla and SpaceX, was another signal that Musk sees his companies as potentially more effective when working together.

Musk said on Tuesday a full merger between the two companies would make sense for the work each is doing around chips, artificial intelligence, software and more.

Musk, who became the world's first paper trillionaire after the SpaceX stock market debut earlier this year, said he is not included in either of the special committees considering the mega-merger.

He described himself as a "conflicted party" as the chief executive of Tesla and of SpaceX.

Even commenting on the possibility of a merger between the two companies, Musk compared to "tap dancing through a minefield".

He added a merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders. At least 50% of Tesla's shareholders would need to approve the merger, which Musk described as "quite a high hurdle to achieve".

Shareholders have supported Musk's desires before. Last year, a majority of investors in Tesla approved a compensation package for Musk valued around $1 trillion.

While Tesla is known as an electric car company, Musk has lately been shifting resources there to work around robotics.

articles.title: Meet Kailyn Brown, the third-grader who won $25,000 for inventing animal-shaped patches designed to make injections less stressful for children
articles.summary: For children who are nervous about needles, a routine visit to the doctor can bring an uncomfortable wait before an injection.
articles.body: For children who are nervous about needles, a routine visit to the doctor can bring an uncomfortable wait before an injection. Kailyn Brown, a schoolgirl from Columbia, South Carolina, knows the feeling herself. Rather than simply putting up with it, she began thinking about something that might make the experience easier for other children. Her idea became Sticky Pals with Magic Medicine, a concept for skin patches shaped around friendly characters that could help numb the area before a shot. Brown, who was in the third grade when she developed the idea, went on to win $25,000 in the kindergarten-to-fourth-grade business category of the Mott Million Dollar Challenge.How Kailyn Brown turned her fear of injections into Sticky PalsBrown did not begin with a business plan or a complicated medical problem to solve. She started with something familiar from her own life: she disliked getting injections. The discomfort gave her a reason to think about what might help children facing the same experience, and she came up with Sticky Pals with Magic Medicine.The proposed product combines a numbing patch with a character designed to make the process less intimidating for young patients. In her interview with Mott, Brown described the idea as a formulated patch applied to the skin to numb the area where a person would receive a shot. Although children were the main audience, she also envisaged versions that could appeal to teenagers and adults.How Sticky Pals patches aim to ease needle anxiety in childrenThe characters are central to Brown's concept. She introduced two of her creations, Chelsea the Unicorn and Dino the Dino, in a demonstration of how the product might be used in a medical setting. The idea is to give children something familiar and approachable to focus on while a healthcare professional prepares the injection.In her demonstration, Brown explained that the patch would be placed over the area where the patient was due to receive a shot. The needle would then pass through an opening at the character's mouth, making the animal figure part of the process rather than simply a decoration on the skin.How Kailyn Brown prepared pitch for the $25,000 business competitionBrown had to record her pitch video several times before she was happy with it. In the first few attempts, she spoke too quickly, then slowed down too much in the next recordings. Getting the pace right took some practice, and she later said she had learned not to give up when something needed repeating.Her aunt helped put the pitch together, while her mother listened as she practised at home. Brown worked on it every Tuesday and Thursday, going through five or six pages of notes. She also got advice from Elizabeth at VentureLab before travelling to Flint, Michigan, to present Sticky Pals in person to the competition judges.Kailyn Brown explains how a growth mindset helped shape her Sticky Pals inventionAs part of the final pitch, contestants were asked to identify an entrepreneurial trait they had demonstrated during the process. Brown chose a growth mindset, connecting it to the way people approach problems and learn from them.She explained the idea through the image of a stone in someone's path. A person could try to kick it away or remove it, she suggested, but another approach would be to learn how to climb over it. Her comparison reflected the way she had worked on Sticky Pals, refining the pitch and responding to feedback rather than treating the first attempt as the finished product.Winning $25,000 opens the next chapterBrown won the grand prize of $25,000 in the K–4 business category of the Mott Million Dollar Challenge. The award recognised her entry in a competition that gives young students an opportunity to present business ideas, explain the problems they aim to solve and develop their skills as entrepreneurs.

articles.title: Falling water levels at Utah’s Great Salt Lake exposed mysterious circular mounds; freshwater springs beneath them may supply up to 12% of the lake’s water budget
articles.summary: Satellite images from 2025 show dozens of circular mounds exposed by falling water levels.
articles.body: Satellite images from 2025 show dozens of circular mounds exposed by falling water levels. Satellite images revealed these features across Farmington Bay, Ogden Bay and Bear River Bay. The mounds stood out from the surrounding dry lakebed, with dense reeds growing at their centres. Researchers traced this unusual vegetation to freshwater springs flowing directly into the lake basin.The discovery points to an extensive underground freshwater reservoir that scientists had not previously recognised. According to Nasa Earth Observatory, the springs may account for as much as 12% of the lake’s total water budget, far above the roughly 3% previously assumed by hydrologists.Satellite images uncover strange circular mounds at Great Salt LakeAs Great Salt Lake’s water levels fell, dozens of unusual circular features emerged along the eastern edge of its drying lakebed. They appeared in parts of Farmington Bay, Ogden Bay and Bear River Bay, where satellite images captured areas that had previously been underwater.University of Utah researchers had encountered possible signs of these features years earlier while travelling by airboat through the lake’s shallow bays. They noticed circular patterns disturbing the water’s surface but could not explain their cause. As more of the lakebed became exposed, similar shapes appeared in images captured by Landsat and other satellites.A Landsat 9 image taken on September 13, 2025, showed at least seven features clustered in Ogden Bay. An image of the same area from September 15, 2011, showed how higher water levels had concealed them.How did researchers investigate the mysterious mounds at Great Salt LakeThe unusual satellite images prompted researchers to organise field expeditions to investigate several features. They travelled across thick patches of reeds to reach the centres of the vegetation-covered mounds, using snow bikes and garden tools to avoid damaging the exposed lakebed.William Johnson, a geologist at the University of Utah, said, "It took some work to reach certain sites since we wanted to avoid using vehicles or other modern equipment that might damage the playa”.Once at the sites, researchers installed piezometers and other monitoring equipment at different depths and distances from the centres of the features. These instruments helped them measure the pressure and salinity of the underlying water. The measurements revealed a clear pattern. Groundwater was salty towards the edges of the mounds but fresher near their centres, where phragmites reeds grew in circular formations.What could hidden freshwater springs reveal about Great Salt LakeThe reeds help distinguish the mounds from the surrounding bright playa in satellite images. Researchers identified dozens of these features, while higher-resolution satellite sensors revealed dozens of smaller examples to the southwest and south of the main cluster.After conducting aerial electromagnetic surveys, the team estimated that probably hundreds of groundwater-fed oases could be spread across newly exposed sections of Great Salt Lake’s playa. Johnson described the features as ‘windows’ into an extensive underground freshwater reservoir that scientists had not previously realised existed. The discovery also changed estimates of how much groundwater enters the lake.Researchers estimate that freshwater discharge from these springs may account for as much as 12% of Great Salt Lake’s total water budget. This is considerably higher than the roughly 3% that hydrologists had previously assumed these springs contributed, highlighting the significance of the newly identified freshwater inflow.Freshwater springs may help reduce dust from the drying lakebedJohnson said the newly identified freshwater inflow could have practical benefits, particularly in limiting dust generated by exposed sections of the lakebed. He cautioned that the discovery did not represent a vast new freshwater resource suitable for large-scale extraction. Dried lakebeds can produce substantial amounts of dust because they contain fine-grained sediments and have little vegetation to hold the material in place. Surface water makes it harder for winds to lift dust and fuel dust storms.

articles.title: SpaceX and Tesla boards form special committees to review merger | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Elon Musk likes the idea but says he is not on either committee, which is made up of independent directors.
articles.body:
The boards of SpaceX and Tesla have each formed special committees to review a possible merger. The special committees, which consist of independent directors, were created at the request of shareholders, according to Elon Musk, CEO and the largest individual shareholder of both companies.

“Because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees, so it’s this sort of a … it’s an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking, and I can’t be in the conversation,” Musk said in response to a question during SpaceX’s third-quarter earnings call.

Musk didn’t name the members of these special committees, only noting that they were independent directors. Tesla has seven independent board members under Nasdaq’s listing standards, including board chair Robyn Denholm, Ira Ehrenpreis, who is also a committee chair, former Tesla CTO JB Straubel, Joe Gebbia, Jack Hartung, James Murdoch, and Kathleen Wilson-Thompson, according to the company’s October 19 proxy filing .

Neither Musk, nor his brother Kimbal Musk, are independent. Denholm, Gebbia, Ehrenpreis, Hartung, Murdoch, and Wilson-Thompson sit on a variety of established committees overseeing audit, compensation, and corporate governance.

SpaceX lists six independent directors , including Ehrenpreis, who is also the chair of the company’s compensation and nominating committee. Randy Glein, Donald Harrison, Steve Jurvetson, Luke Nosek, and Roelef Boutha are also considered independent directors.

Antonio Garcias, Musk, and SpaceX president and chief operating officer Gwynne Shotwell are also on the board, but not considered independent. Garcias, who once sat on Tesla’s board, founded and leads Valor Equity Partners, which has a 3.4% stake in SpaceX. Garcias’ firm also financed SpaceX’s AI hardware purchases through leaseback arrangements.

Musk said he supports the idea of the merger, but cautioned that it is not a guaranteed outcome.

“I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla Motor is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it,” he said, adding that he thinks it would be a good idea. “At the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this.”

The special committees have not reached agreement on the terms of any transactions, he said.

The SpaceX IPO cemented Musk’s grip on the company — he has more than 50% voting power — which would make it easier to garner support for a merger from SpaceX shareholders. It is a much bigger hurdle over at Tesla, where the company would need a 50% vote from all shareholders, not just those who vote, Musk noted.

“I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity,” Musk said, adding there was a lot to be gaining from cooperating on developing AI software, robotics, SpaceX’s orbital AI data center project Starmind, and Terafab, the joint chip manufacturing project between Tesla and SpaceX.

articles.title: Chefe da Ferrari dá nota 10 a Tesla que 'voa' e elogia Elon Musk | G1
articles.standfirst: Benedetto Vigna elogiou tecnologia e apresentação do novo Roadster, que usa propulsores derivados de sistemas da SpaceX para realizar manobras aéreas.
articles.summary: Benedetto Vigna elogiou tecnologia e apresentação do novo Roadster, que usa propulsores derivados de sistemas da SpaceX para realizar manobras aéreas.
articles.body:
O presidente-executivo da Ferrari, Benedetto Vigna, elogiou a apresentação do esportivo Roadster feita pela Tesla na semana passada. A demonstração incluiu manobras aéreas impulsionadas por propulsores derivados de tecnologias da SpaceX e instalados no carro.

Segundo a agência Reuters, o executivo disse que a indústria automotiva ainda tem espaço para inovações ousadas, mesmo em um mercado consolidado. Ele deu nota 10 para a tecnologia e nota 10 para a apresentação.

“Isso certamente mostra que, também no mundo automotivo, ainda há muito a ser feito. Temos que continuar sonhando ", disse Vigna.

Vigna elogiou a iniciativa durante uma entrevista por videoconferência a uma conferência automotiva organizada pela revista italiana "Quattroruote". Na ocasião, o executivo defendeu que as montadoras precisam assumir riscos e buscar ideias fora de seus próprios ambientes .

“Como europeu, obrigado por nos mostrar como, mesmo em um mundo antigo, ainda é possível inovar e ousar”, disse o presidente da Ferrari.

Tesla Roadster flutua na rampa — Foto: divulgação/Tesla

Elon Musk , presidente-executivo da fabricante, afirmou que a produção do Roadster começará em 2028.

A reação do mercado financeiro foi mista. As ações da Tesla subiram inicialmente, mas analistas avaliaram que a entrega do carro ainda está distante, após anos de tentativas frustradas de tirar o projeto do papel.

A Tesla apresentou em outubro a versão do Roadster , equipada com vários sistemas que são novidade no mercado. Um deles é um mecanismo de sucção com ventiladores. A tecnologia cria downforce para grudar o carro no chão, permitindo fazer curvas em alta velocidade.

Durante a demonstração oficial da Tesla, o veículo conseguiu escalar paredes e até ficar de cabeça para baixo.

Tesla Roadster na versão Rocket consegue flutuar com sistema de ar comprimido da SpaceX. — Foto: Divulgação / Tesla

O carro conta com mais de 1.300 cavalos de potência, somente com tração traseira. O modelo adota uma tecnologia da Tesla com um sistema de propulsores capaz de fazer a aceleração de 0 a 100 km/h em menos de um segundo.

Na versão Rocket, o veículo consegue descarregar dois tanques de ar comprimido para realizar manobras aéreas.

Na apresentação do modelo, o esportivo usou essa tecnologia para pular e dar uma pirueta por cima de todos os carros da Tesla.

Tesla Roadster faz de 0 a 100 km/h em menos de 1 segundo. — Foto: Divulgação / Tesla

A Ferrari ganhou as manchetes recentemente com um carro eletrificado que chamou a atenção não por voar, mas pelo seu design polêmico. As ações da empresa despencaram após a revelação do carro.

Apresentada ao público, a Ferrari Luce instantaneamente virou um meme na internet . O modelo traz um desenho arredondado e proporções que quase não lembram os tradicionais esportivos de luxo da marca italiana.

A fabricante diz que, mesmo assim, o interesse pela Ferrari Luce foi muito grande . O esportivo tem um custo de quase US$ 600 mil.

Ferrari também causou polêmica com seu carro elétrico, o Luce. — Foto: divulgação/Ferrari

O desenvolvimento do modelo contou com a participação de Jony Ive , ex-chefe de design da Apple, e da equipe de seu estúdio, a LoveFrom.

Para Vigna, a colaboração com profissionais de fora da indústria automotiva foi importante para chegar ao resultado desejado. O executivo afirmou que trabalhar apenas com a equipe interna não teria produzido as mesmas respostas.

“Se tivéssemos trabalhado sozinhos, não teríamos feito o que fizemos. Em outras palavras, enfrentamos toda uma série de questões e chegamos a algumas respostas estimuladas por pessoas que nos observavam de fora”, afirmou.

O executivo participou da entrevista por videoconferência, diretamente da Índia, onde a Ferrari organizou um evento para clientes. Ele também disse que o interesse pela marca italiana no país era forte.

articles.title: Quote of the day by Stephen Hawking: “We are just an advanced breed of monkeys on a minor planet of…” - understand why humans are special despite living on a tiny planet
articles.summary: Look up at the night sky and it's hard not to feel a little small. Earth is one planet.
articles.body: Look up at the night sky and it's hard not to feel a little small. Earth is one planet. It goes around a star that, honestly, isn't anything unusual, and that star isn't even near the middle of our galaxy. Past our solar system there are billions more stars, and galaxies so far away their light left them before humans existed. Still, here we are, asking how all of it works. And getting real answers.That's the idea Stephen Hawking packed into one line. He's humbling us and cheering us on in the same breath. We barely register in the cosmos. Yet we've managed to figure out how the universe began, what stars are doing and how space and time behave. Not bad for a species from a small rocky planet.There's something in it for everyday life as well. We aren't the biggest animals around, or the strongest. What we do have is the urge to look past today's problems, check the evidence and keep learning.Quote of the day by Stephen Hawking“We are just an advanced breed of monkeys on a minor planet of a very average star. But we can understand the Universe. That makes us something very special.”What is the meaning of Stephen Hawking’s quotePut simply, Hawking is comparing two things. How tiny we are. And how much we can understand anyway.The "advanced breed of monkeys" part is about our origins. Humans are primates. Millions of years of evolution shaped us, just like every other living thing on Earth. We're part of nature, not something standing outside it.Then he zooms out. Earth is a "minor planet". The Sun is an "average star". Our planet is home, sure, but in the Milky Way it's a speck. The Sun is one star among a huge crowd, and the Milky Way is one galaxy among countless others we can see.But the second half of the quote turns everything around. Small as we are, we can study the very universe we're sitting in.We work out how planets move. We catch light from galaxies millions of light years away. We study black holes and dig up clues about what the early universe was like. Our brains grew up here, on this one planet. The questions they ask don't stay here.So what's he really saying? Size isn't everything. We're small, and we understand a surprising amount. Both things are true.Why Hawking compares humans with monkeysWhy monkeys, of all things? Because it keeps us honest about where we came from. We didn't just appear one day. We share common ancestors with other primates, and our story is one chapter in the much longer story of life. (Scientists would point out that humans are grouped with apes, not monkeys. Hawking wasn't giving a biology lesson, though. He was making a point about our roots.)It's a gentle jab at the idea that humans are somehow above everything else.Our intelligence is impressive, no question. It still came from the same natural processes that shaped every other species. Telescopes, maths, space probes: all of it traces back to life on Earth.And we're still fragile. We need the right air, water and temperature to survive, and there's plenty about our own planet we haven't figured out yet.Does knowing all this make human achievement less impressive? Not at all. It makes it more amazing. Creatures that evolved in one small corner of space have worked out how to study places they'll probably never visit.What does the quote mean by a “minor planet” and an “average star”Here Hawking is putting Earth and the Sun in their place, so to speak.Earth orbits the Sun. The Sun is one of the many stars in the Milky Way, and it sits well away from the galaxy's centre. Our whole solar system takes up a tiny part of it. Many of those other stars have planets of their own."Average" doesn't mean every detail of the Sun is boring. Astronomers call it a main-sequence star, and its size and mass sit somewhere in the middle of the wide range of stars out there. That's all Hawking means.Neither Earth nor the Sun is at the centre of anything. People once believed Earth was. Then Copernicus suggested the Sun was at the centre, and later astronomers found that even the Sun is just one star in a vast galaxy.Hawking's wording follows that long shift. The universe wasn't built around us. Earth matters hugely to us, but that doesn't put it at the centre.Funny, though. This "minor" planet is where the people who worked all this out came from.Why understanding the universe makes humanity specialHawking isn't claiming the universe was made for us. His point is about what we can do. We can look into how reality actually works.Think about the tools we've made. Telescopes let us see things our eyes never could. Spacecraft have flown past, orbited and landed on other worlds. In 2015, detectors picked up gravitational waves for the first time, tiny ripples in space from two black holes colliding far away. And mathematical models let scientists test ideas about things no lab could ever recreate.None of this happened overnight. It took curiosity, people working together and knowledge handed from one generation to the next.Usually it goes something like this. Someone proposes an idea. Someone else builds a way to test it. Then others take those results and ask the next question. Ideas get checked, argued over and improved along the way.And it's not finished. Nobody fully knows yet what dark matter is, what's driving dark energy, or exactly what happened in the universe's first moments. Honestly, that's part of the fun.We don't know everything. But we know when we don't know something, and we know how to go looking. That's the special part.The importance of curiosity and asking questionsCuriosity gets a big shout-out in this quote too, and it deserves one.So many discoveries start with a simple "why?" Why do planets move like that? What are stars made of? How did the universe get to where it is now? What happens to stuff that falls into a black hole?Some of these sound like questions with no practical use. Then, years later, they lead somewhere nobody expected.Being curious stops us from settling for the first easy answer. It makes us look at the evidence, test what we assume and stay open to being surprised.You see this outside science all the time. Take a student who asks why a maths formula works. They'll usually understand it far better than someone who just learns it by heart. Or someone at work who questions the "way we've always done it" and finds a better way. A researcher who follows up on a strange result might find something everyone else walked past.Asking questions is one of the most useful things we do. Hawking clearly thought so.Why humility is essential to knowledgeRead the quote again and there's a small warning in it. If you want to understand the universe, you have to accept how much of it is beyond you.Once people decide they already know enough, they stop listening to new evidence. Being humble keeps that door open.Science works because ideas can be tested, and changed if they fail. A theory has to survive tough questions. New observations can force scientists to update what they thought. Changing your mind when the evidence says so? That's not losing. That's the whole method.Same thing in daily life. Admit a mistake and you get the chance to fix it. Hear out someone who disagrees and you might learn something. Say "I'm not sure" and you've taken the first step to finding out.Hawking wants us to hold two thoughts together. We're clever. And we still have a lot to learn.How to apply Stephen Hawking’s quote in daily lifeStay curious: When something catches your attention, ask about it. Don't just accept the first explanation you hear.Keep learning: Knowledge isn't a box you tick once. Keep coming back to it.Be willing to admit uncertainty: "I don't know" is a perfectly good starting point.Look beyond immediate concerns: A bad day feels smaller when you remember the bigger picture.Respect evidence: Know the difference between what you know and what you're guessing, and be ready to change your view when better information shows up.Value collaboration: Big discoveries often come from people sharing ideas and building on each other's work.How the quote changes our perspective on human achievementWe tend to measure success in terms of money, status, power or fame. Hawking offers another way to look at it.What we've achieved isn't impressive because Earth is big. It isn't. Or because the Sun is mighty. It's a fairly ordinary star. It's impressive because life on this planet learned to understand things far beyond its own backyard.The universe's history is far, far older than human civilisation. Even so, we've found ways to piece parts of it together from the clues around us today.Have we mastered the cosmos? Not even close. But we've made a real start.Why Stephen Hawking’s words remain relevantWhy do people still share this quote? Because it gets at two questions we haven't stopped asking. Where do we fit in the universe? And what should we do with the time and knowledge we've got?Astronomy keeps showing us just how complicated the cosmos is. New planets keep turning up around other stars. Telescopes keep getting better at seeing distant galaxies. Each discovery answers something, and usually raises a new question or two.It's also a healthy way to look at our own lives. Feeling small can make us more humble. It doesn't have to make us feel pointless.A human life is a blink in cosmic time. But in that blink we can be curious, make things and understand things. We can learn how life became possible, figure out how nature works and pass all of it on to the next generation.And progress only happens if we keep asking. Understanding the universe is a long project. It needs patience, evidence and people working together.The deeper lesson behind the quoteHawking brings humility and wonder together in just a few words. We came from nature. We live on a small planet orbiting one star among many. And yet the universe produced us, beings who can study how vast and complex it really is.Being small and being capable aren't opposites. They actually go together. The more we learn about the universe, the more we realise how much we still don't know.So stay curious. Trust evidence. Value what you learn. And remember that you don't have to be at the centre of everything to matter.The key takeaway? Humanity doesn't matter because of the size of our planet or our spot in the cosmos. We matter because we can question, learn and understand. We're a tiny part of a huge universe, and we can still explore its mysteries. That alone is a good reason to stay curious and keep looking for answers.

articles.title: Tesla and SpaceX: Why does Elon Musk want to merge the companies?
articles.summary: Musk says there's "a lot to be gained" by combining the firms in what would be the biggest merger in history.
articles.body:
Elon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he is considering bringing them together .

Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes."

The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed.

With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5tn (£1.1tn) and SpaceX at $2tn (£1.5tn), a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever.

Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together.

"In my opinion, 100%. It's just a question of when," says David Nicholson, the Chief Technology Advisor at The Futurum Group, a market research company.

The unveiling of the Tesla Roadster last week - a futuristic electric car powered by SpaceX rocket thrusters - served as a "symbolic embodiment" hinting at the two Musk companies merging, Nicholson said.

Musk, the CEO of both SpaceX and Tesla, said bringing the firms together would be beneficial given the work each does around chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology projects.

Specifically, the deal would combine Tesla's cars, robots and self-driving technology with SpaceX's rockets, data centres, satellites and telecommunications operations.

The move could be a step towards Musk's mission to build a self-sustaining city on Mars - a vision that has invited sceptics but also plenty of backers.

Over the past year, Musk has moved to consolidate his businesses, with SpaceX acquiring xAI and X, formerly Twitter, before going public this year.

But the merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, with half of Tesla's needed to back the deal, a threshold even Musk described as "quite a high hurdle". Musk, as CEO of both companies, cannot participate in shareholder discussions.

Even so, Musk, a key shareholder of Tesla, will likely get his way in the next few years, said investment analyst Dan Sheehan from Telos Wealth Advisors.

He believes shareholders will back the deal as the technology the companies develop complement each other, Sheehan said.

But the merger would mean that Tesla shareholders will likely hold a "smaller slice of a much larger and more complex business," he added.

"There's no real precedent for how a public company like Tesla gets priced in this," Sheehan said.

SpaceX shares rose 8% in after hours trading while shares of Tesla climbed by 1.5%.

Experts told the BBC that Tesla drivers are unlikely to see much drastic change in the near term, even if the two companies combine.

In fact, vehicles seem almost like "an afterthought", overshadowed by the potential to combine the Tesla and SpaceX's tech capabilities, Nicholson said.

Changes are already underway at Tesla. The carmaker said earlier this year that it would prioritise its best-selling Model Y and Model 3, shifting focus away from less popular models .

Tesla also started using a manufacturing plant in California to produce humanoid robots, known as Optimus.

Pairing Tesla's self-driving technology and robotics with SpaceX's AI and satellite network could result in more capable vehicles, Sheehan said.

"The question is how much priority cars get inside a company increasingly driven by AI infrastructure," he added.

The recent Roadster showcase suggests SpaceX technology could be pulled into future Tesla products, which could attract more customers, said Tu Le, the founder of advisory firm Sino Auto Insights.

The Cybertruck-maker faces intense competition from Chinese carmakers like BYD, which overtook Tesla as the world's biggest EV maker in January.

The biggest winner is probably Musk - the world's richest man who also became the world's first trillionaire earlier this year.

The merger would give Musk greater voting control over the combined company than he currently has at Tesla, a factor the special committee assessing the deal would have to consider.

A single company makes it easier for Musk to run his AI strategy the way he wants, Sheehan said.

"The deal itself doesn't add to Musk's wealth, but it concentrates it further in one stock," he said.

Elon Musk's stratospheric rise to trillionaire status - in charts

Who is Elon Musk and what is his net worth?

However, the merger could attract scrutiny over Musk, already a polarising figure in the US, Nicholson said.

The move could also face more regulatory pressure if Democrats - many of whom have been critical of Musk - win more seats in the US midterm elections next month.

Shareholders have backed Musk's desires before. Last year, Tesla investors approved an unprecedented compensation package for Musk valued around $1tn .

"I honestly don't think Musk will be keeping track of what the merger will do for his wealth," Nicholson said.

The deal also brings Musk closer to what Nicholson says is "his mission in life": colonising Mars.

articles.summary: La Liberty Bell 7 se hundió en 1961 tras un accidente durante la recuperación del astronauta Gus Grissom
articles.body: La conquista del espacio también está marcada por misiones que terminaron de una forma inesperada. Una de ellas fue la de la Liberty Bell 7, una cápsula estadounidense que desapareció bajo las aguas del océano Atlántico después de completar su vuelo espacial en julio de 1961. Su recuperación parecía una tarea extremadamente complicada, pero casi cuatro décadas después un equipo de exploradores logró localizarla y devolverla a la superficie. La nave había transportado al astronauta Gus Grissom durante un vuelo suborbital de aproximadamente 15 minutos, dentro del programa Mercury de la NASA. Aunque la misión se desarrolló con normalidad durante el trayecto espacial, todo cambió cuando la cápsula amerizó y comenzó la operación para rescatar tanto al astronauta como a la nave. El problema comenzó cuando la escotilla de la Liberty Bell 7 se abrió de manera inesperada después del amerizaje. El agua empezó a entrar en el interior de la cápsula y Grissom tuvo que abandonarla rápidamente para evitar quedar atrapado. El astronauta consiguió mantenerse a flote, aunque su traje comenzó a llenarse de agua y su rescate se convirtió en una operación de emergencia. Un helicóptero logró sacar a Grissom del océano, pero recuperar la nave resultó mucho más complicado. El aparato intentó elevarla mediante un cable, aunque el peso adicional del agua que había entrado en su interior superó su capacidad de carga. Para evitar poner en peligro a la tripulación, los equipos tuvieron que soltarla. La cápsula se hundió y quedó a unos 4.900 metros bajo la superficie del océano Atlántico. La búsqueda no dio resultados hasta 1999, cuando una expedición financiada por Discovery Channel utilizó sistemas de sonar y vehículos submarinos teledirigidos para localizarla. Tras identificar su posición, el equipo organizó una operación de recuperación que culminó el 20 de julio de ese año, exactamente 38 años después de la misión original. Una vez en la superficie, la cápsula fue trasladada para someterla a un minucioso proceso de conservación y restauración. Los especialistas comprobaron que algunos materiales habían resistido sorprendentemente bien el paso del tiempo bajo el agua, aunque las piezas metálicas presentaban corrosión. Actualmente, la Liberty Bell 7 se conserva en el museo Cosmosphere, en Kansas, donde permite conocer uno de los episodios más singulares de los primeros vuelos espaciales tripulados.

articles.title: El desierto más árido de la Tierra se ha cubierto de flores silvestres: “Es un fenómeno único; hay más de 200 especies de plantas”
articles.standfirst: Un suceso que impacta y cubre una de las zonas más secas del planeta
articles.summary: Un suceso que impacta y cubre una de las zonas más secas del planeta
articles.body: En Chile ha llegado la primavera y, con ello, un cambio de tiempo evidente en esta época del año en el hemisferio sur. Cerca del océano Pácífico y la cordillera de los Andes se ubica el desierto de Atacama, el cual cubre unos 1.600 kilómetros. En este punto, uno de los más áridos que se conocen, donde uno esperaría encontrar una gran extensión de tierra seca, han aparecido una enorme cantidad de flores silvestres. Si bien este fenómeno puede ser común con el cambio de estación, no lo es tanto en un área en la que lo habitual es ver grandes escenas rocosas. Ahora, este proceso se le conoce comúnmente como ‘Desierto Florido’ y ha sorprendido incluso a los propios ciudadanos locales. La culpa de esto, al parecer, es la enorme cantidad de lluvias producidas en la región entre los meses de julio y agosto, donde incluso se registraron algunos récords nunca superados desde que hay datos de 1950. “Desde que se tienen registros de precipitaciones, estas son las cifras más significativas en términos de volumen: 160, 180, 190 milímetros en algunos lugares”, asegura César Pizarro, jefe de la Sección de Conservación de la Biodiversidad de Conaf Atacama, en palabras recogidas por The Star. Los expertos relacionan este aumento de los chubascos con el fenómeno de ‘El Niño’ más extremo de los últimos años y esto, a su vez, deriva en el ‘Desierto Florido’ más intenso desde 1997. Pizarro señala que estas lluvias activaron el material conocido como germoplasma, que incluye semillas, bulbos y tubérculos, así como huevos de invertebrados y reptiles. “Hay colinas y sierras donde no se ha visto vegetación ni flores en más de 30 o 40 años. Este germoplasma del desierto puede permanecer latente durante muchos años, incluso décadas. Las colinas de este año son el mejor ejemplo de ello”, sostiene el experto, que apunta que se han podido ver especies como terciopelos naranjas o garras de león, entre otras.

articles.title: Florida scientists tracked 142 invasive Burmese pythons for 20 years and found that all four expelled tracking devices came from pregnant females
articles.summary: Scientists tracking invasive Burmese pythons in southern Florida recorded four cases of implanted tracking devices being expelled during a study spanning
articles.body: Scientists tracking invasive Burmese pythons in southern Florida recorded four cases of implanted tracking devices being expelled during a study spanning 2005 to 2024. The study examined 305 transmitters implanted in 142 adult snakes across Big Cypress National Preserve and Everglades National Park. According to the report published in the Journal of Animal Biotelemetry, titled ‘Case report: observations on expulsions from 20 years of radiotransmitter implantation in adult Burmese pythons’, the research found that all four expulsions involved gravid females with intramuscularly implanted transmitters. No transmitter-related deaths were observed. The researchers also examined whether reproduction and implantation methods could influence device retention, noting that both surgical techniques were effective for monitoring adult pythons.How many Burmese python tracking devices were expelled in FloridaOf the 305 transmitters implanted during the study, 221 were placed intramuscularly, while 84 were positioned inside the coelomic cavity. The researchers reported that four transmitters were expelled, representing 1.3% of the total. All four cases involved intramuscularly implanted transmitters in gravid females, meaning females carrying developing eggs. No transmitter-related deaths were observed among the study animals.The four expulsions occurred in females that had received their implants in late January or early February, during the breeding season, which runs from December to March. The devices were expelled before the females laid their eggs. The researchers recorded the expulsions between 57 and 111 days after surgery, with a reported mean of 101 days. The paper’s abstract summarised the findings: “Overall, 98.7% of transmitters were retained, with a 1.3% expulsion rate (n = 4 transmitters).” The researchers also reported that the four cases occurred among 13 gravid females in the relevant group, while other gravid females retained their transmitters and subsequently laid clutches of eggs.How did four Burmese pythons lose their implanted tracking devicesThe paper describes four individual cases involving female pythons in Big Cypress National Preserve. In the first case, a female measuring 414 centimetres in snout-to-vent length and weighing 42 kilograms received two transmitters on 26 January 2006. When researchers recaptured her on 17 May that year, she had a clutch of 46 eggs, and one transmitter was lying on the ground nearby. Both devices had been detected at her previous location two days earlier. An examination found no abscesses or skin wounds, leaving the mechanism of expulsion unknown. The researchers recorded the event 111 days after surgery.The other three cases involved females implanted in January or February 2022. In one case, a female measuring 450 centimetres and weighing 81.2 kilograms had a transmitter visible through an open skin abscess on 1 April, approximately 80 days after implantation. The animal was removed from the field for surgery as the abscess enlarged. A replacement transmitter was implanted on 29 April, and the female laid 81 eggs on 23 May. In the fourth case, a female measuring 441 centimetres and weighing 73.6 kilograms had a transmitter visible through an open abscess on 1 April, 57 days after surgery. The transmitter was replaced on 29 April, and the python laid 96 eggs between 21 and 23 May. The researchers also documented an earlier case in which a transmitter was partially expelled through an open skin abscess 155 days after surgery. These observations show that the circumstances surrounding expulsion differed between individual snakes, including whether an abscess or visible wound was present.Why might pregnant Burmese pythons be more likely to expel devicesThe researchers said the low expulsion rate indicated that both intramuscular and coelomic implantation techniques were effective for monitoring adult Burmese pythons. However, they identified a possible association between transmitter expulsion and the reproductive status of females. In their discussion, they wrote: “This suggests that some gravid females may be at a higher risk for expelling transmitters, compared to males or non-gravid females.” They proposed that changes associated with reproduction, including possible changes in immune response and pressure within the body cavity, might contribute to the risk. These explanations were presented as possibilities rather than established causes.The study also found that all four expelled devices had been implanted intramuscularly. The authors suggested that placing transmitters inside the coelomic cavity might reduce the risk of expulsion in gravid females, but stressed that the number of recorded cases was small. They noted that the cause of expulsion could involve abscess formation at the incision site rather than the timing of implantation relative to egg-laying. Their conclusion stated: “We observed no mortality related to transmitter implantation and few instances of transmitter expulsion, indicating that both intramuscular and coelomic implantation techniques are effective for monitoring adult pythons in the wild.” The authors added that their findings may inform research on other large-bodied snake populations where radiotransmitter implantation is appropriate and feasible.
